Damaged remains of an under-construction building after it partially collapsed in the Paharganj area, New Delhi, on November 15, 2026. | Photo Credit: PTI
A day after an under-construction hotel building collapsed in Delhi’s Paharganj, leaving eight workers injured, the Delhi Police apprehended the property owner and contractor on Monday (November 16, 2026), bringing the spotlight back on rampant safety violations at construction sites across the Capital.
The two accused, identified as Raman and Anwar, were booked under Sections 290 (negligent conduct with respect to buildings), 125(a) (act endangering life or personal safety), 223(a) (disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to DCP (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh.
The construction was also underway despite a ban on outdoor construction imposed as part of measures to curb air pollution, making it only one of the violations among many others.
The property owner, Raman (left), and contractor Anwar (right) of the building that collapsed in Central Delhi’s Paharganj, injuring 8 people on November 15 | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement
The incident came just 10 days after seven workers were killed when an “unauthorised” three-storey building under construction collapsed in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar .
The recurring incidents have exposed a pattern of unsafe construction, inadequate safeguards and weak enforcement, with violations coming into focus only after a collapse claims lives.
But for the workers who build the city, unsafe conditions are not confined to the moments when a structure gives way. Missing helmets, inadequate protective equipment, long working hours and contractors racing against deadlines are part of their everyday working conditions, they told The Hindu.
“Basic safety equipment, including industrial shoes, gloves, uniforms and good-quality helmets, is not provided by contractors. They simply tell us, ‘Jo hai bas aajao ’ [come with whatever you have],” said Raja, a construction worker from Mandawali who was also at the Chawri Bazar site on November 5.
The safety gear, he said, is sometimes brought out only when an inspection or an official visit is expected. Workers are asked to wear uniforms that otherwise remain unavailable to them.
Buildings with four or five storeys are now being put up in as little as 20-25 days, he said, with contractors assigning work in the morning and expecting it to be completed by the end of the day. “We work at least 12 hours a day with only half a day off on Sundays to earn around ₹17,000-18,000 a month. We don’t know what will happen at work which will claim our lives,” he said.
NDRF personnel conduct a search and rescue operation at the site after a three-storey building under construction collapsed, killing at least two people and trapping several under the debris, at Chawri Bazar in New Delhi on November 06, 2026. | Photo Credit: Shashi Shekhar Kashyap
Delhi Fire Service Divisional Fire Officer A.K. Jaiswal, who has led rescue operations at several such incidents, said even elementary safety precautions were frequently missing at work sites.
“Helmets, safety shoes and goggles are basic requirements, but these too are not available, forget about the safety precautions and first aid on the site. The focus is on money; safety is not even the last concern,” he said.
“Until an incident happens, everyone thinks nothing will happen,” he said, adding that workers themselves sometimes resisted using protective equipment despite being advised to do so. However, he said, contractors were responsible for ensuring that workers were provided with and used safety gear, and should not allow work to proceed without it.
The rush to complete projects also compromises structural safety, Mr. Jaiswal said. Weak beams and slabs, inadequate structural checks and insufficient time for concrete to settle can undermine a building’s stability. Contractors often rush to lay the next roof slab without allowing the previous one sufficient time to set and strengthen, he said. Workers at heights, meanwhile, frequently lack full-body safety harnesses to prevent fatal falls.
At many sites, even first-aid facilities and stretchers are missing. The absence of adequate open spaces and exit routes can also make it difficult for workers to escape during an emergency and for rescue teams to reach them when a collapse occurs, he noted.
An injured foot of a rescued worker at the site after a three-storey building under construction collapsed, killing at least two people and trapping several under the debris, at Chawri Bazaar, in New Delhi, Thursday, November 5, 2026. | Photo Credit: PTI
The enforcement gap is particularly concerning given that construction continues despite restrictions, said Professor Siddheshwar P. Shukla, a member of the Delhi Construction Workers Board. He alleged that contractors were pushing workers into basements and other enclosed or hazardous spaces to circumvent the outdoor construction ban, exploiting their financial vulnerability.
“Even large construction companies are not providing adequate safety measures. In several cases, workers die, the companies pay some money and send the bodies back to their hometowns. Many such deaths go unreported,” he alleged.
Mr. Shukla said 12-hour shifts were increasingly becoming the norm, with workers effectively being paid “minimum wages on paper” for extended working hours. He called for the Delhi Construction Workers Board to step in and provide protective equipment where employers failed to do so, while holding owners and contractors accountable.
Subhash Bhatnagar, coordinator of the National Campaign Committee for Construction Labourers, said the repeal of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, had weakened safeguards for construction workers.
“The Act was introduced after years of struggle to secure workers’ rights and provide a framework for regulating their employment and safety. It contained more than 200 provisions relating to construction workers’ safety, several of which are no longer available under the new framework,” he said.
The Act, along with the Building and Other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Act, 1996, was replaced by the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, and the Code on Social Security, 2020, which came into effect on November 21, 2025. Mr. Bhatnagar argued that the new framework had diluted several safeguards, while the shift towards monetary penalties and compliance notices had weakened deterrence against violations.
He also questioned the effectiveness of safety committees envisaged under the new framework, particularly for the numerous small-scale residential construction sites across Delhi that do not employ large workforces.
“What is needed is an effective inspection mechanism to ensure that the laws are implemented. The penalty for violating safety norms must be considerably higher than the cost of providing safety equipment,” he said.
As buildings continue to rise across the Capital, the recurring collapses are exposing a crisis that remains largely invisible until a structure comes down, and the people who built it are left buried beneath the rubble.
